newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy faces crisis of confidence.
newsitem.headline: German economy faces crisis of confidence.

text.p: The German economy, Europe's biggest, is stuck in a psycholigical mire where a climate of gloom is creating a self-fulfilling prophecy that is preventing growth and jobs from picking up, economists say.
"The key right now is sentiment," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economsit at UBS. "As long as sentiment does not change, the economy will not get any better."
Two economic announcements on Thursday should give everyone in Germany from consumers to captains of industry little reason break out of their malaise.

The Federal Statistics Office announced that economic growth in 1996 slowed to 1.4 percent from 1.9 percent in 1995 and the Federal Labour Office reported that December unemployment rose 48,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.156 million.

The economists said that, simply put, the cycle of pessimism which led to the weak economic data runs like this -- Consumer spending, the biggest part of the economy, has been held back by high unemployment. Unemployment, however, is largely the result of companies' reluctance to invest. But companies will not invest until consumption picks up.
"As the economic outlook is still gloomy, the German unemployment problem cannot be solved this year," Trinkaus Capital Management wrote in a commentary.
Growth in private consumption in 1996 sunk to 1.4 percent in 1996 from 1.8 percent the year before.
Economists said the key to breaking out of the blues is Germany's export sector.
Historically, Germany's growth cycle has started with exports which jump-start growth as companies increase investment to meet fresh demand.
Consumer spending, the final phase of the business cycle, normally clicks in once investment creates new jobs and higher wages.
But exports have taken longer to break that cycle this time round than they have in the past.

Although foreign demand has remained relatively strong, companies have until only recently been nervous about investing because of the strength of the mark and because German labour costs are among the highest in the world.
Economists said, however, that exports might finally be ready to play their historical role as economic primer.
"We are seeing the first faint signs that export growth is starting to feed through into the domestic economy," said Brian Clapp, economist at Stone & McCarthy.
While an upturn in exports failed to ignite the economy in 1994, economists are more hopeful that strong foreign demand for German products will spur growth.
They said that a stronger dollar, record low interest rates and low wage increases are making companies more confident, boosting their will to increase spending.
"Corporate sentiment will be helped by exports," Fahrinkrug said. "That should help the investment pillar of the economy to pick up."
